data.title: Goldman Sachs Turns Bullish on Palantir Stock – Here’s Where the Upside Lies
data.description:
Palantir (NASDAQ:PLTR) is bucking the trend today (Thursday, Oct. 8), with shares moving higher despite the market’s downturn. The stock was one of the biggest early winners of the AI trade, and has been gathering steam again recently after a period of lagging the broader tech market, approaching the all-time high set a little under a year ago. Shares are now up around 18% this year, a respectable return, but that still trails the Nasdaq-100’s ~23% gain.

Much has been made of Palantir’s frothy valuation, although the company has still been delivering exceptional growth. So, does that relative underperformance mean expectations around Palantir have actually become too cautious?

Goldman Sachs analyst Gabriela Borges thinks they have. As such, Borges has upgraded Palantir from Neutral to Buy and raised her price target from $204 to $230, representing around 15% upside from current levels. (To watch Borges’ track record, click here)

Promotion

Curious why XOVR invested in Kalshi? Explore the long-term strategy behind the investment.

The 5-star analyst believes Palantir could enter another phase of outperformance through 2027, driven by a bigger addressable market and an FDE model that competitors might find harder to replicate than it appears.

The first part of the thesis is the changing nature of enterprise AI. Borges argues that 2025 and 2026 were largely about relatively standardized applications such as coding, customer service and experimentation. The next phase could be much more valuable, with companies using AI against their own proprietary data, workflows and decision-making processes to strengthen their competitive advantages.

That plays directly into Palantir’s strategy around sovereign AI and bespoke applications. Instead of replacing core systems such as ERP or CRM, enterprises can build specialized AI software on top of their existing infrastructure. Borges believes Palantir’s Ontology gives it an advantage here by connecting enterprise data with real-world objects, relationships and workflows, making that information usable by both humans and AI.

The opportunity could be substantial. Borges estimates Palantir’s SAM (serviceable addressable market) could eventually reach around $500 billion before accounting for the amount of an enterprise’s software and services budget one vendor can realistically capture. Applying a 10% ceiling brings that figure down to roughly $50 billion, or about $35 million per Global 2000 company, compared with Palantir’s current annualized commercial revenue per customer of around $4 million.

The second debate is whether Palantir’s forward-deployed engineers, or FDEs, are becoming a commodity. Microsoft, Salesforce and Snowflake are all developing similar capabilities. Borges argues that Palantir’s advantage is not simply having engineers working alongside customers. Its FDEs feed customer-specific insights back to product teams, which turn those solutions into reusable software that can then be deployed across an industry.

That feedback loop is being augmented by AI. Palantir’s AI FDEs and AIP Evolve can automate parts of deployment, testing, workflow analysis and optimization, allowing knowledge accumulated across customer engagements to scale without requiring equivalent growth in human engineers.

Government contracts provide another potential catalyst, with TITAN entering production, Maven moving toward a formal Program of Record and Palantir playing a central role in the Army’s Next Generation Command and Control architecture.

Borges acknowledges that government spending can be lumpy, but believes Palantir’s technology, commercial expansion and accumulated deployment expertise justify a more bullish stance.

The Goldman view gets support from 16 other bullish reviews, while an additional 4 Holds and 2 Sells all add up to a Moderate Buy consensus rating. However, the $204.15 average price target implies shares will stay rangebound for the time being. (See PLTR stock forecast)

data.title: Oracle or Apple: Two Very Different AI Bets, But Only One Stock Is a Buy, Says Daniel Ives
data.description:
Oracle (NYSE:ORCL) and Apple (NASDAQ:AAPL) are taking almost opposite approaches to the AI opportunity. The former is spending enormous sums to build the infrastructure behind the AI boom, with capital expenditures reaching levels that are putting pressure on its cash flow and balance sheet. Apple, by contrast, stands out among the major technology companies for not having to make anything close to the same kind of massive AI infrastructure investment. While Oracle is spending billions on data centers, GPUs and cloud capacity, Apple can potentially monetize AI through the enormous ecosystem it has already built.

That makes the two stocks very different ways of investing in the AI theme. Oracle is making a capital-intensive bet that demand for AI computing will justify the cost of building out capacity. Apple is betting that AI can make its existing hardware, software and Services ecosystem more valuable without requiring a similar spending spree. Both have compelling arguments, but the risks sit in very different places.

Yorkville Ives & Co analyst Dan Ives has been taking the measure of both, and thinks the investment case differs right now.

Promotion

200% short exposure to ORCL with ORCZ

Ives believes Oracle has secured a strong position in AI infrastructure. Oracle Cloud Infrastructure is attracting major training and inference workloads, while its Database@ strategy allows the company to monetize database demand even when customers use AWS, Azure or Google Cloud. Together with Fusion, NetSuite and Oracle Health, Ives sees a broad AI monetization opportunity.

The concern is what it will cost to capture that opportunity. Oracle expects $90 billion to $95 billion of capital expenditure this fiscal year, while free cash flow is negative and debt has reached $125 billion. Project Jupiter, a 2.45-gigawatt New Mexico campus, has also faced delays involving its gas pipeline and permits. Oracle has issued a force majeure notice to the project’s infrastructure provider, highlighting the risks involved in delivering capacity on schedule.

Those risks matter given Oracle’s $664 billion RPO, much of which depends on new infrastructure coming online as planned. Financing is also becoming more expensive. Oracle’s 10-year bonds yield roughly 7.4%, compared with a 4.87% weighted average coupon on its existing debt, while five-year credit-default swaps have reached roughly 245 basis points. S&P’s BBB- rating leaves the company only one notch above speculative grade.

The demand itself is not the problem. First-quarter revenue jumped 30% to $19.35 billion, cloud revenue rose 62% to $11.6 billion, and OCI infrastructure revenue surged 121% to $7.4 billion. GPU utilization reached 97.9%, and Oracle raised its fiscal 2027 outlook to at least $90 billion of revenue and $8.10 in non-GAAP EPS. The issue for Ives is whether Oracle can execute the infrastructure buildout without putting too much pressure on its finances.

“We see a company with the right assets and a balance sheet that has moved ahead of its ability to control the build, and we rate the shares IN LINE (i.e., Neutral) until execution catches up.

That In Line rating comes with a $155 price target, implying 10% upside for the shares over the coming months.

Apple offers something completely different. With more than 2.5 billion active devices, including roughly 1.5 billion iPhones, Apple already has an enormous audience for AI. Ives believes Apple Intelligence and AI-powered Siri can embed AI into everyday consumer activity while strengthening the company’s existing Services ecosystem. Rather than selling AI infrastructure, Apple can potentially use AI to increase engagement, drive upgrades and create new monetization opportunities across health, fitness, finance, gaming and other areas.

That could become particularly important for Services. Ives estimates AI-influenced revenue could eventually add more than 15% to Services revenue, an opportunity he believes the market has not fully reflected in Apple’s valuation. He puts the potential AI contribution at around $75 per share, effectively arguing that Apple’s AI opportunity is an additional source of value layered on top of an already enormous business.

Then there’s the hardware opportunity. Ives reckons around 375 million iPhones have gone more than four years without an upgrade, creating a substantial replacement pool as the iPhone 18 cycle develops. He believes the new Duo foldable could also begin a fresh hardware cycle, with roughly 10 million units possible initially and as many as 15 million in a stronger scenario. “In our view,” Ives concluded, “Apple is moving into a new stage of its ecosystem story, one in which AI ties hardware, software, and services together and becomes the trigger for both device upgrades and higher monetization per user and drives the next leg of the Cupertino growth thesis.”

Accordingly, Ives rates the stock as Outperform (i.e., Buy). His $400 price target offers one-year upside of 19%.  

Turning now to the rest of the Street’s views, we find ORCL stock claims a Strong Buy consensus rating, while its $242.62 average price target points to 12-month returns of 71%. AAPL is rated a Moderate Buy, although its $337.51 average target suggests the shares are fully valued. (See Oracle stock forecast or Apple stock forecast)

data.title: ‘Look Out Below,’ Says Investor on Micron Stock
data.description:
As far as its business is concerned, everything seems to be going right for Micron (NASDAQ:MU). Memory prices are surging, AI demand remains enormous and the company is generating eye-watering amounts of cash. The problem is that this is exactly what the top of a memory cycle can look like.

So says investor Gil Rotstein, who believes Micron might be getting closer to that point. The argument is not that AI demand is collapsing or that Micron is a weak company. Instead, the concern is that today’s exceptional earnings are being driven heavily by pricing, while new supply is approaching and customers are already finding ways to use less memory.

No doubt, the numbers are highly impressive. Micron generated $133.2 billion of revenue in fiscal 2026, around 3.6 times that of the prior year. Its latest quarter produced $54.2 billion of revenue, an 87% gross margin and $33.2 billion in free cash flow. Management expects $61.5 billion of revenue and $38.15 in EPS next quarter, above analyst expectations.

Promotion

Curious why XOVR invested in Kalshi? Explore the long-term strategy behind the investment.

Yet Rotstein thinks the details matter more than the headline numbers. DRAM revenue increased 27% sequentially, but bit shipments rose only in the mid-single digits. Prices, meanwhile, jumped by the high teens. In other words, much of the growth is coming from higher prices rather than substantially greater volumes.

The supply shortage is particularly severe because of high-bandwidth memory (HBM), which is essential for AI accelerators but consumes considerably more production capacity than conventional DRAM. More HBM therefore means less capacity available for other memory products.

Micron’s customers are already feeling the pressure. Nvidia has warned that extreme memory pricing is hurting margins, while Broadcom has also cited increasing memory content as a profitability headwind. Outside AI, the impact is even clearer. Micron reported declining mobile and client bit shipments, AMD expects higher memory costs to weigh on PC demand, and IDC forecasts an 11.3% decline in PC shipments this year.

AI demand remains strong, but customers are beginning to optimise their memory usage too. AMD has said customers are looking for ways to reduce their memory footprint, suggesting that scarcity is changing purchasing behaviour even in AI infrastructure.

Then there is supply. New capacity is expected to begin coming online from mid-2027. Rotstein believes that could eventually put pressure on pricing and margins, following the familiar memory-cycle pattern of shortages, higher prices, capacity expansion and eventual oversupply.

The valuation adds to the concern. Micron trades at roughly 6.1 times forward earnings and 4.9 times forward EV/EBIT, well below key peers. But it trades at about 9.1 times trailing sales, far above the sector median. For Rotstein, that combination suggests investors are valuing Micron on peak profitability.

With EPS expected to fall substantially after the next few years, Rotstein sees limited upside despite the company’s excellent fundamentals. Contracts, price protections, the prospect of buybacks and strong AI demand provide support, but the risk-reward is no longer compelling enough.

Accordingly, Rotstein rates the stock a Hold (i.e., Neutral). (To watch Rotstein’s track record, click here)

However, most on the Street disagree. Based on a mix of 26 Buys and 1 Hold, the stock claims a Strong Buy consensus rating. At $1,630.19, the average price target implies shares will climb 53% higher over the coming months. (See Micron stock forecast)

data.title: Think Differently About Sandisk Stock, Says Investor
data.description:
From a traditional standpoint, Sandisk (NASDAQ:SNDK) is the kind of memory stock investors approach with caution. NAND is notoriously cyclical, and strong pricing can disappear quickly when supply catches up with demand. But the market is starting to look different as hyperscalers become a much bigger part of the customer base.

What was once a highly cyclical business dominated by smartphones, PCs and consumer electronics is becoming much more strategically important as hyperscalers build out massive data-center infrastructure. That shift is giving memory suppliers greater negotiating power and customers a stronger incentive to secure supply well in advance.

The scale of those commitments is becoming difficult to ignore. Sandisk now has $93.9 billion of contracted NBM business, covering more than half of its expected FY2027 bits and roughly two-thirds of FY2028 bits. More importantly, customers have provided about $16.5 billion in deposits, credits and third-party financial guarantees against those commitments, with $2.5 billion already received in cash. That financial backing represents roughly 18% of the remaining contract value, providing meaningful protection if customers fail to follow through.

Promotion

Two ETFs to trade SNDK long or short: SNXX & SNDQ

An investor using the pseudonym High Alpha Professor (HAP) argues that this distinction matters because customer funding can otherwise make Sandisk’s cash generation look stronger than it really is. The company reported $11.49 billion of free cash flow for FY2026, but $2.48 billion came from NBM prepayments and deposits. After excluding that money, along with another $275 million related to Flash Ventures, adjusted free cash flow was $8.74 billion. In other words, the underlying business is still producing substantial cash without relying on customer advances.

The same trend is appearing at Micron, where the number of Strategic Customer Agreements (SCAs) and associated financial commitments has expanded rapidly. But HAP sees Sandisk’s model as particularly compelling because the financial backing behind its remaining NBM obligations has risen faster than the contract book itself.

The reason is the changing customer base. A smartphone manufacturer can delay purchases or reduce memory usage when prices rise. A hyperscaler building a data center cannot simply leave storage out of the system. Sandisk’s data-center revenue surged from $325 million in FY2024 to $5.15 billion in FY2026, making the segment roughly a quarter of annual revenue and nearly a third in the latest quarter.

That shift gives customers a good reason to pay for reliable supply and gives Sandisk greater leverage over pricing. HAP therefore expects contracted volumes to keep expanding, provided suppliers retain control of the market.

Valuation also looks less demanding if the current economics persist. Sandisk’s latest guidance implies roughly 9.5 times annualized quarterly earnings. HAP stresses that this would normally be a dangerous way to value a cyclical memory stock, but the NBM contracts and pricing floors could make the current earnings level more durable than in previous cycles.

The key test is margins. Sandisk expects roughly 80% non-GAAP gross margins through FY2028-FY2030, while near-term guidance suggests little deterioration despite further revenue growth. If those margins hold, HAP believes the stock remains attractive. If they begin falling sharply, the investment case becomes considerably less compelling.

“For now,” the investor concluded, “I remain a Buy because the contracting model is still expanding while floor economics remain exceptionally strong.” (To watch High Alpha Professor’s track record, click here)

That take sits well with most of the Street’s analysts covering this stock. Based on a mix of 15 Buys and 2 Holds, the consensus view is that this name is a Strong Buy. Over the next year, shares are expected to appreciate by 34%, given the average price target clocks in at $2,205.59. (See SNDK stock forecast)

data.title: Alphabet or Nvidia: One AI Stock Is a Compelling Buy, the Other’s Issues Can’t Be Ignored, Says Top Investor
data.description:
Alphabet (NASDAQ:GOOGL) and Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) are both major names associated with the AI boom, but they offer investors very different ways to play it. Alphabet is trying to turn its AI capabilities into another growth engine across Search, YouTube, cloud and enterprise services. Nvidia, meanwhile, remains the dominant supplier of AI accelerators powering the industry’s infrastructure buildout.

Looking at the investment case for both of these AI giants, top investor Envision Research believes the important question is not simply which company has the stronger AI position.

The comparison comes down to several factors, including not only the strength of each company’s AI opportunity, but also its ability to turn that opportunity into earnings growth, and the valuation investors are being asked to pay. The 5-star investor also sees important differences in the risks facing the two businesses, particularly Alphabet’s ability to translate Gemini’s progress into commercial growth and Nvidia’s inventory and supply-chain pressures.

Promotion

200% short exposure to NVDA with NVDS

For Alphabet, Envision sees its Gemini 4 Argon model as an important catalyst. The investor points to its strong benchmark performance against competing models across areas including knowledge work, agentic coding and cybersecurity. However, Envision’s interest goes beyond benchmark rankings. The investor believes Gemini could become more valuable when combined with Google’s existing products and infrastructure, potentially helping Alphabet secure large enterprise contracts while improving engagement and monetization across Search and YouTube.

The investor is also particularly impressed by Alphabet’s returns on capital. Envision calculates Alphabet’s TTM (trailing twelve months) ROCE (return on capital employed) at 64.7%, compared with an average of around 56.6% over the previous five years. Alphabet is simultaneously investing heavily in AI infrastructure, with Envision’s estimated reinvestment rate currently close to 50%.

Envision does not expect that reinvestment rate to remain so high. The investor models an average rate of around 25% over the next five years, which, combined with the current return on capital, could support organic growth of roughly 16%. That is important because Envision does not believe investors are paying an excessive price for that potential growth.

The stock trades at around 16.6x forward earnings in Envision’s model. At the investor’s expected growth rate, that produces a PEG ratio of approximately 1x, which Envision considers an attractive level for a GARP (growth-at-a-reasonable-price) investment.

To this end, Envision Research rates GOOGL stock a Buy. (To watch Envision Research’s track record, click here)

Nvidia presents a more complicated picture. Envision acknowledges that the company’s financial performance remains extraordinary. Revenue increased 105% year over year in the latest quarter, with the company once again beating expectations.

But the investor is less focused on Nvidia’s headline growth than on what is happening to its inventory. Inventory turnover has fallen well below its recent three-year average of around 4x, indicating that Nvidia is converting inventory into sales less efficiently than it has historically.

Envision believes there are reasons to expect continued pressure. Memory and substrate constraints could require Nvidia to hold additional inventory. The investor also notes that higher HBM prices could increase the dollar value of Nvidia’s inventory even if the company is holding the same number of physical units, potentially putting further pressure on inventory-turnover metrics. Envision sees these supply-chain issues as potential pressure points for Nvidia’s profitability metrics.

Envision is also cautious about the stock’s near-term technical setup. With NVDA trading close to its all-time highs, the investor believes the shares could spend some time consolidating rather than immediately continuing higher.

That does not mean Envision considers Nvidia expensive. The investor estimates that NVDA trades at roughly 25x forward earnings, only a modest premium to the sector median. More importantly, Nvidia’s earnings growth could justify that multiple. Management expects more than 70% growth for FY28, while consensus estimates imply roughly 95% EPS growth. On a growth-adjusted basis, Envision therefore still considers Nvidia’s valuation attractive.

However, while Nvidia offers extraordinary growth, the investor sees the other issues as reason for caution. “The upbeat growth is offset by both fundamental uncertainties (such as the slowed inventory turnover, memory and substrate wafer constraints, etc.),” Envision summed up. “Combined with the technical signs, we see good odds of consolidation in the near term.”

Accordingly, Envision rates NVDA a Hold (i.e., Neutral).

The Street, however, takes a bullish stance on both these names, rating the pair as Strong Buys. NVDA’s average price target lands at $324.20, suggesting shares have 12-month upside of 38%. Meanwhile, GOOGL is expected to gain 21%, considering the average target clocks in at $427.04. (See GOOGL stock forecast or NVDA stock forecast)

data.title: ‘It’s Only a Matter of Time,’ Says Investor About Oracle Stock
data.description:
For a while it looked like Oracle (NYSE:ORCL) was poised to be one of the market’s AI winners, but that moment turned out to be fleeting. From one of the hottest AI infrastructure plays, Oracle has become one of the more heavily questioned software names. After a strong run in late 2025, the stock has fallen more than 56% from its peak as investors have shifted their attention toward Oracle’s enormous capital requirements and the risks surrounding its AI expansion.

That pessimism has left Oracle trading at a valuation that looks relatively modest compared with its growth prospects. Based on forward earnings estimates, the stock trades at roughly 17.8 times FY27 earnings and just 13.2 times FY28 earnings.

Investor Gary Alexander views those multiples as attractive for a company with Oracle’s growth potential, recurring revenue base and rapidly expanding infrastructure business. In his view, the market is placing too much weight on Oracle’s financing needs while failing to fully account for the earnings potential of its massive AI backlog.

Promotion

200% short exposure to ORCL with ORCZ

There are several reasons for investors to remain bullish, according to Alexander. First, Oracle is not simply an AI infrastructure company. Its cloud applications continue to produce double-digit growth, with its Fusion suite expanding at a healthy pace. NetSuite has been weaker, partly because customers have delayed larger IT decisions while assessing the impact of AI, but the upcoming NetSuite Next release could provide a catalyst by embedding more AI and automation into its ERP (enterprise resource planning) products.

The bigger story, however, is infrastructure. Oracle’s RPO (remaining performance obligations), effectively its contracted backlog, jumped by $26 billion to $664 billion in the latest quarter. Much of the new business is structured through customer prepayments, “bring your own hardware” arrangements and similar models, reducing the amount of capital Oracle needs to provide upfront. At the same time, contractual margins are improving.

Alexander is particularly encouraged by the economics of Oracle’s existing infrastructure. Contracts are being renewed at roughly 20% higher prices on average, while GPU capacity is being utilized at an exceptionally high 97.9%. Even older GPUs are retaining value, with renewed or resold capacity generating premiums over previous contracts.

Oracle also delivered 30% year-over-year revenue growth in Q1, accelerating sharply from the previous quarter. Adjusted earnings per share rose 31%, comfortably beating expectations. With more data-center capacity coming online, Alexander expects this acceleration to continue.

The main concern remains financing. Oracle still faces a substantial funding requirement to support its capital expenditure, while debt has already reached roughly $125 billion. Higher interest rates and floating-rate exposure could put pressure on profitability and cash flow.

“That said,” the investor summed up, “I also think risks are reflected in Oracle’s modest valuation, while accelerating revenue growth and operating profit also help to plug an increasing share of the company’s capex needs and funding hole. Stay long here and use the dip as a buying opportunity.”

Accordingly, Alexander rates ORCL stock a Buy. (To watch Alexander’s track record, click here)

That’s what most of the Street’s analysts think too. Based on 27 Buys, 5 Holds and 1 Sell, the stock claims a Strong Buy consensus rating. Going by the $242.62 average price target, shares will be changing hands for a 69% premium a year from now. (See Oracle stock forecast)

data.title: ‘The Penny’s About to Drop,’ Says Top Investor About Micron Stock
data.description:
Micron (NASDAQ:MU) investors have cut a frustrated bunch since the company reported earnings last week. The memory giant had just delivered another exceptionally strong quarter, yet the muted reaction left some wondering whether the AI trade is finally losing momentum.

However, buoyed by a new Street-high price target issued today (Wednesday, Oct 7) by a Wall Street analyst, the stock is once again pushing higher.

That move will certainly make sense to investor James Foord. Foord, who ranks among the top 2% of investors on TipRanks, remains bullish on the stock and believes Micron is still undervalued. The argument rests not just on earnings growth, but also on the company’s improving visibility and potential for substantial shareholder returns.

Promotion

Curious why XOVR invested in Kalshi? Explore the long-term strategy behind the investment.

Micron’s latest quarter once again exceeded expectations, with revenue, gross margin and earnings all coming in above the top end of management’s previous guidance. Revenue jumped 31% sequentially and 379% year over year, marking the company’s sixth consecutive quarterly record.

Digging into the details, the numbers were just as impressive. DRAM revenue reached $39.8 billion, while NAND generated $14.1 billion. Data-center SSD revenue was almost $10 billion, more than ten times higher than a year earlier, while the Core Data Center business grew 56% sequentially with a 90% gross margin.

The balance sheet has also become a major strength. Micron finished the fiscal year with $73.5 billion in cash and investments against just $5.2 billion of debt. Foord sees the slightly weaker first-quarter gross margin as a temporary issue related largely to incentive compensation and inventory accounting rather than a deterioration in the underlying business.

More importantly, Micron’s future revenue is becoming easier to see. The company has signed 26 strategic customer agreements covering more than 35% of revenue through 2030, while more than 75% of its 2027 shipments are already committed. Management also expects supply conditions to become substantially tighter in 2027 and 2028, with meaningful new capacity unlikely to arrive until 2028 or 2029.

There is a bear case around Micron, and Foord acknowledges the risks. Higher prices could encourage competitors such as Samsung and SK hynix to add capacity, while changes to Nvidia’s future architectures could reduce HBM requirements. A slowdown in hyperscaler spending could also trigger a valuation reset even if Micron continues delivering strong earnings.

Still, Foord believes the valuation leaves plenty of room. Currently, Micron trades at roughly 14 times trailing earnings. Under the investor’s base case, earnings could reach about $170, meaning a $1,500 share price would require only around a 9x earnings multiple.

There’s also a potential catalyst in shareholder returns. With free cash flow potentially exceeding $100 billion after capital expenditure, Foord expects substantial buybacks to begin once the current CHIPS Act restriction expires on December 9. Management has indicated that it intends to return excess cash to shareholders over time, making the end of the restriction a potentially important catalyst for the stock.

“As far as I can see, there’s nothing wrong with Micron or the memory cycle,” the 5-star investor summed up. “The company keeps beating its own guidance, and we still have no evidence of a slowdown in memory demand or prices. The contracts give us incredibly clear visibility as far as 2030, and even if the cycle slows down thereafter, with all the cash and buybacks the company can carry out, the stock should easily keep trending upward.”

To this end, Foord rates the stock a Strong Buy. (To watch Foord’s track record, click here)

The analyst consensus has reached the same conclusion, a rating based on a lopsided mix of 26 Buys vs. 1 Hold. The average target stands at $1,630.19, a figure pointing to 12-month returns of 51%. (See Micron stock forecast)

data.title: Down More Than 50%, Is Rocket Lab Stock Now a Coiled Spring? Top Investor Lays Out the Catalyst
data.description:
Rocket Lab (NASDAQ:RKLB) has become one of the market’s more interesting pure-play space companies, combining rocket launches with a much broader space-systems business.

Revenue is surging, its backlog has reached record levels, and the company is building an integrated operation that stretches from satellite components to launch services.

The problem is that Rocket Lab is still a high-risk growth story. The stock has fallen more than 50% from its 2026 high as investors digest delays to its much-anticipated Neutron rocket and the enormous cost of bringing it to market.

Promotion

70% Off TipRanks

  • Unlock powerful investing tools with TipRanks Premium to make smarter, more confident investment decisions
  • Subscribe to TipRanks Smart Investor Newsletter, and discover new investing opportunities with data-backed stock picks
Learn more about TipRanks Premium

For top investor Andres Cardenal, however, that pullback makes the risk-reward more attractive, particularly if Neutron delivers.

Rocket Lab has two main businesses: Launch Services and Space Systems. Electron remains the company’s established small-lift rocket, giving customers dedicated access to low Earth orbit rather than forcing them to share a ride and then maneuver their satellites into position. The company also operates HASTE, a modified Electron used for hypersonic testing, an area receiving substantial attention from the U.S. government.

The bigger opportunity is Neutron. The medium-lift reusable rocket is designed to carry much larger payloads and compete for satellite-constellation launches. Its development has been delayed, making a successful first flight one of the most important catalysts for the stock.

Cardenal, who ranks among the top 1% of investors on TipRanks, also sees Space Systems as an important part of the story. Rocket Lab manufactures components including solar panels, reaction wheels and satellite separation systems, while its Photon platform allows it to build complete spacecraft for customers. This creates a business that is less dependent on the economics of launching rockets and can generate more predictable, multi-year revenue.

Meanwhile, the company keeps on delivering strong financial results. Q2 revenue jumped 62% to $234 million, while the company secured $437 million of new launch contracts and finished the quarter with a $2.36 billion backlog, up 137% year over year. The planned Iridium acquisition could further strengthen the business while adding to cash-flow generation.

That said, Rocket Lab is burning significant amounts of cash to fund Neutron, new launch infrastructure and manufacturing capacity. Free cash flow is expected to remain deeply negative in 2026 before improving and turning positive later in the decade. The 5-star investor believes the company’s $2.4 billion cash and securities balance gives it substantial room to execute.

Nevertheless, while it is also the big catalyst, Neutron remains the biggest risk. Delays have already pushed the original timeline back considerably, with the first launch now potentially arriving in late 2026 or 2027. Competition from SpaceX is another major concern, given its enormous scale and Starship ambitions. Government spending is also important because Rocket Lab has significant exposure to defense contracts.

For Cardenal, Rocket Lab is obviously not a defensive stock or a predictable compounder. It is a high-risk bet on the expansion of the space economy, but one worth taking.

“The most exciting part is that the company is becoming a fully vertically integrated space exploration leader, and it is facing an inflection point in the near term,” the investor summed up. “If Neutron flies as planned, Rocket Lab stock should take off too.”

To this end, Cardenal rates RKLB stock a Strong Buy. (To watch Cardenal’s track record, click here)

Most Street analysts agree with that take. Based on a mix of 14 Buys and 2 Holds, the stock receives a Strong Buy consensus rating. The forecast calls for one-year gains of 54.5%, given the average price target stands at $110.07. (See RKLB stock forecast)

data.title: ‘Open Your Eyes,’ Says Top Investor About Oracle Stock
data.description:
Oracle (NYSE:ORCL) has been undergoing a major transformation. Once primarily known as an enterprise software company, it is becoming a much more significant player in cloud infrastructure, with its AI-related business growing at a far faster rate than the rest of the company. Yet the stock continues to trade at a valuation that suggests investors remain deeply skeptical about whether Oracle can successfully execute this transition.

That skepticism is understandable. Although the underlying growth numbers are difficult to ignore, Oracle has taken on substantial debt to fund its infrastructure expansion, while a large portion of its massive backlog is tied to OpenAI.

But that is actually one reason why investor Julian Lin, who ranks among the top 2% of investors on TipRanks, is particularly bullish on Oracle. He sees improving fundamentals at OpenAI and believes the AI company’s recent progress strengthens the case that Oracle can ultimately deliver on its enormous infrastructure commitments.

Promotion

200% short exposure to ORCL with ORCZ

Lin’s confidence is based partly on the scale of Oracle’s backlog. Management expects revenue growth of up to 34% in the next quarter and has guided for full-year revenue of at least $90 billion, alongside as much as $95 billion in capital expenditure. The spending is enormous, but Lin argues that investors should focus on what the infrastructure buildout can become once these projects are operational rather than simply focusing on the near-term cash requirements.

Free cash flow is currently a major weakness. Oracle’s balance sheet ended the quarter with $37.1 billion of cash and marketable securities against $125.3 billion of debt. The infrastructure expansion is also putting pressure on cash generation. However, management has indicated that as projects ramp up, the company expects to move toward a much stronger free cash flow conversion rate and eventually reach a self-funding position.

Lin sees that potential improvement as an important part of the investment thesis. Oracle’s infrastructure business may carry lower gross margins, but management has pointed out that it also requires substantially less spending on R&D and sales. As a result, Lin believes investors should pay greater attention to operating margins rather than focusing exclusively on gross margins.

The other major concern is Oracle’s dependence on OpenAI. A substantial portion of the company’s backlog is connected to the AI company, creating obvious customer concentration risk. If OpenAI were unable to sustain its growth or meet its computing commitments, Oracle could face a significant problem.

Lin, however, believes the latest developments at OpenAI make that risk look less threatening. OpenAI’s annual revenue run rate has reportedly climbed to $70 billion, while the company has continued expanding its consumer and enterprise offerings. Lin is also encouraged by OpenAI’s ability to compete with Anthropic in enterprise development. In his view, the recent improvement in OpenAI’s competitive position makes it more likely that the company will be able to support the enormous computing demand underlying Oracle’s backlog.

Meanwhile, Oracle continues to trade at a relatively modest valuation. The stock is valued at roughly 17x forward earnings, while Lin estimates that it trades at only around 9x expected 2029 earnings. For Lin, that disconnect is central to the investment case: the market is assigning a relatively low valuation to a business whose fastest-growing segment is expanding at triple-digit rates and whose backlog provides substantial visibility into future revenue.

Oracle still carries considerably more risk than the other major hyperscalers. Its debt burden increases the consequences of poor execution, while its dependence on a single major customer creates additional uncertainty. The company also needs to execute an extremely ambitious infrastructure buildout without allowing its balance sheet to become an even greater constraint.

But that risk is exactly why the 5-star investor believes the valuation is attractive. Oracle is being treated as though its infrastructure strategy could fail, while its fastest-growing business is moving in the opposite direction. If Oracle can continue converting its enormous backlog into revenue, improve free cash flow as its infrastructure projects mature, and maintain OpenAI as a strong and growing customer, the current valuation could prove difficult to justify.

To this end, Lin rates ORCL stock a Strong Buy. (To watch Lin’s track record, click here)

data.title: It’s Almost Time for Sandisk Stock, Says Investor
data.description:
Sandisk (NASDAQ:SNDK) has plenty going for it right now. The memory market is showing much more strength than many investors expected, pricing remains elevated and the current cycle could stay favourable for longer. For Sandisk, that creates a promising backdrop for earnings and cash generation.

However, things are not quite as simple as that. The stock has had a mega-run and already reflects much of the improvement, while its valuation premium over memory peer Micron leaves less room for error. Sandisk’s contracts offer some protection if conditions deteriorate, but they also limit how much of a further pricing surge the company can capture.

For an investor using the moniker The Alpha Analyst (AA), that makes the stock an interesting case of a strong business operating in a strong market, but at a price that still demands some caution.

Promotion

High conviction on SNDK? Try Tradr's SNXX or SNDQ

The investor now believes the balance is shifting. Sandisk is not quite cheap enough to warrant a Buy, but the stock is getting close to that point.

AA’s view has become more constructive as the memory outlook has strengthened. Micron’s latest results offered further evidence that the upcycle could remain tight through 2027 and 2028, with NAND prices rising roughly 30% sequentially. Pricing, rather than shipment growth, continues to do much of the heavy lifting.

That is positive for Sandisk, but it does not capture the entire benefit. A large portion of Sandisk’s supply is covered by contracts with pricing floors and caps. These agreements provide greater stability, but also limit the company’s ability to benefit fully if memory prices continue climbing. Sandisk also uses DRAM in its SSD products, meaning tight DRAM markets can push up its costs.

That trade-off is important when looking at Sandisk’s valuation. The stock trades at roughly a 35% premium to Micron on an EV-to-forward-EBITDA basis, partly because its contractual protections should make earnings more resilient when the memory cycle turns. The investor believes that premium is reasonable, but it has yet to be tested. The real question is whether those protections will deliver as expected when additional industry capacity comes online later in the cycle.

For now, the growth outlook remains strong and Sandisk is returning substantial amounts of cash through buybacks. The company repurchased roughly $4.5 billion of stock against around $5 billion of free cash flow in its latest quarter.

That gives the stock some support, but the valuation remains the main obstacle. The investor believes Sandisk’s premium to Micron needs to be justified, particularly given the cyclical nature of the memory business and the fact that its contractual advantages have yet to be tested.

The upcoming earnings report could beat expectations, given the strength across the memory industry, but one strong quarter is unlikely to settle that longer-term question.

For now, for The Alpha Analyst the stock remains a Hold, although the investor believes it is getting close to becoming a Buy. A pullback toward $1,600 would provide the additional valuation cushion needed to make the risk-reward more attractive. (To watch The Alpha Analyst’s track record, click here)

data.title: Tesla Stock Is Only for the Unrealistically Optimistic, Says Top Investor
data.description:
Tesla (NASDAQ:TSLA) launched the Cybercab in September, bringing its autonomous ride-hailing ambitions closer to the real world and giving investors a clearer look at what could become one of the company’s biggest new businesses. The autonomous ride-hailing opportunity is potentially enormous, and Tesla has one obvious advantage: its ability to manufacture vehicles at scale and potentially do so more cheaply than dedicated autonomous-driving rivals.

But the size of the opportunity is not the same thing as the value available to shareholders. The key question is how much of the robotaxi market Tesla can realistically capture, and whether that is enough to justify the stock’s already demanding valuation.

Investor James Foord, who ranks among the top 2% of investors on TipRanks, takes a broadly positive view of the Cybercab’s prospects, but his valuation work leads him to a much more bearish conclusion on Tesla stock. Foord believes the company would need to capture roughly half of the autonomous ride-hailing market to make the current share price look compelling.

Promotion

TSLQ: built for a short position on TSLA

The Cybercab does have a genuine cost advantage. Tesla’s biggest strength in robotaxis could be its manufacturing economics. Unlike Waymo, which relies on expensive vehicles fitted with autonomous-driving technology, Tesla controls much more of the vehicle production process itself.

Foord estimates that a Cybercab could eventually have a significantly lower cost per mile than competitors. That matters because autonomous taxis could operate at fares well below today’s ride-hailing prices while still generating attractive margins.

Tesla also has two potential business models. It could own and operate large Cybercab fleets itself, keeping the economics of each ride, or create a platform where Tesla owners put their vehicles into the robotaxi network and Tesla takes a percentage of the fares. The latter would allow faster expansion but would leave less profit with Tesla.

Foord’s valuation model looks out to 2036 and considers different levels of market growth and Tesla’s eventual market share. His conclusion is that the Cybercab could become a huge business, but the numbers only become truly transformative if Tesla captures an unusually large portion of the market.

At a 50% share in his most optimistic scenario, Foord estimates the business could eventually be worth around $2.7 trillion. Discounted back to today, however, that equates to roughly $268 per Tesla share.

The rest of Tesla does not solve the problem. Foord assigns value to Tesla’s existing automotive business, energy storage, FSD subscriptions and Optimus. Even with bullish assumptions, he arrives at roughly $114 per share for these businesses combined.

Add that to the Cybercab bull case and Tesla reaches around $380 per share, roughly where the stock trades today.

So the problem is that the current valuation appears to require several optimistic assumptions to materialize simultaneously.

Competition makes that harder. Waymo already has a substantial autonomous fleet and significant real-world experience, while Uber controls a huge ride-hailing customer base and is building its autonomous network through partnerships.

Foord’s view is therefore that Tesla could absolutely build a successful robotaxi business, but success alone might not be enough. At the current price, investors need Tesla to execute exceptionally well across several businesses at once.

For Foord, that risk-reward equation is unattractive, leaving him with a Sell rating on TSLA. (To watch Foord’s track record, click here)

Two Street analysts agree with that thesis, but with an additional 13 Buys and 11 Holds, the stock claims a Moderate Buy consensus rating. The average target stands at $396.39, which suggests shares will gain a modest 4% over the coming months. (See TSLA stock forecast)

data.title: Micron Stock Gets a $3,000 Street-High Price Target. ‘Still Misunderstood,’ Says D.A. Davidson
data.description:
Micron (NASDAQ:MU) stock is under pressure today, with shares falling around 2.5% in premarket trading. The immediate trigger is a potential strike at the company’s Taoyuan facility in Taiwan, one of its most important manufacturing hubs. Around 99% of union members who voted backed strike authorisation following a dispute over Micron’s bonus and profit-sharing arrangements. The timing of any strike has not yet been decided.

The stock is also being dragged lower by weakness across the semiconductor sector, while investors remain sensitive to concerns about how long the current memory-price boom can last.

Today’s pullback follows what some Micron investors have seen as a perplexing reaction to last week’s outstanding quarterly readout. But for those concerned about the stock’s performance, the latest note from D.A. Davidson analyst Gil Luria will be extremely reassuring.

Promotion

Curious why XOVR invested in Kalshi? Explore the long-term strategy behind the investment.

Luria recently met with Micron’s investor relations team and came away convinced that shareholders are only beginning to understand the scale of the opportunity. “We concluded that investors are early in their journey of understanding MU’s value and believe that journey will lead them to assigning a far higher multiple,” he said.

As such, Luria reiterated a Buy rating on the stock and raised his price target from $2,100 to a new Street-high of $3,000, suggesting the shares will gain 187% in the year ahead. That target represents roughly 19 times the analyst’s estimated fiscal 2027 earnings. (To watch Luria’s track record, click here)

Luria’s core argument is that more memory makes AI systems better. Larger memory capacity can improve model performance, speed, and context windows, creating a powerful incentive for AI companies to consume more of it. The analyst expects demand to exceed supply through 2027 and 2028.

That is why so-called “de-specing” should not necessarily be viewed as bearish. If Nvidia and other customers temporarily use less memory per system because supplies are constrained, their products may perform worse. That could ultimately encourage them to secure even more memory later.

The analyst uses Tesla as an analogy. If Tesla expected to sell one million cars using large batteries but demand suddenly doubled, it could use smaller batteries to sell more vehicles immediately. The cars would have less range, but Tesla would still generate more revenue overall and would have an even stronger reason to buy batteries in the future.

Luria also sees Micron’s long-term supply contracts, or SCAs (Strategic Customer Agreements), as a major change for the memory industry. Around 50% contracted supply provides visibility without sacrificing all of the upside if demand exceeds expectations. With major customers such as Amazon, Microsoft, Google, Nvidia and Apple, the risk of customers simply abandoning commitments should also be lower than in previous memory cycles.

As for China, it has “been in the math, and is still in the math.” Chinese memory producers are gaining share domestically, but Chinese demand itself is running ahead of supply, meaning the country can continue absorbing their output without necessarily undermining Micron’s broader opportunity.

“This all means Micron is on a growth trajectory for the next 3-5 years, which is what the market has not yet acknowledged,” says Luria.

The company has already indicated that both volumes and pricing could remain favourable through 2028.

Then there is the potential capital return. Once restrictions under the CHIPS Act expire in December, Micron has said it intends to use all excess cash for share buybacks. “If the company chooses the disciplined and opportunistic approach they have demonstrated for their product pricing, we would expect this buyback to become a big challenge for short sellers,” Luria further added.

Luria acknowledges the $3,000 target may look extreme compared with today’s price, but the analyst says he has deliberately stress-tested the thesis and still sees the upside. “We used the last two days as an opportunity to talk ourselves out of this high price target, but were unsuccessful,” Luria summed up. “A company that is well positioned, in an important market, and will grow earnings faster than the market for the next 3-5 years, is likely to trade at least at a market multiple.”

Luria might be the biggest MU bull but he is far from the only one on Wall Street. Based on a mix of 26 Buys and 1 Sell, the stock claims a Strong Buy consensus rating. Going by the $1,630.19 average price target, a year from now shares will be changing hands for a 56% premium. (See MU stock forecast)

The opportunity goes well beyond GPUs. As AI data centers become larger and more complex, they need faster connections between servers, racks and even separate facilities. That is creating demand for high-speed optical components, sophisticated switching technology and custom chips. Marvell has exposure to all three, giving it several ways to benefit from the enormous capital being poured into AI infrastructure.

KR points to AMD’s agreement to acquire World Labs for approximately $8.2 billion in stock. AMD says World Labs’ expertise should help shape its future hardware, software and systems as AI expands into robotics, simulation and physical applications.

data.title: Joby Aviation or Archer Aviation: Which eVTOL Stock Has a Stronger Cash Position? Top Investor Weighs In
data.description:
Joby Aviation (NYSE:JOBY) and Archer Aviation (NYSE:ACHR) are trying to pull off something that sounds almost absurdly ambitious: reshaping short-distance air travel with eVTOL (electric vertical takeoff and landing aircraft), or in layman’s terms, flying taxis. Both companies are making meaningful progress with their eVTOL technology, but turning promising prototypes into viable businesses is another matter entirely.

The problem is that neither company has anything close to the revenue needed to support its spending. Both are pouring enormous sums into R&D (research and development) and the infrastructure required to commercialize their aircraft. That makes cash reserves just as important as technological progress.

Investor Reuben Gregg Brewer, who contributes to The Motley Fool and who ranks among the top 3% of investors on TipRanks, has been taking a closer look at whether either company has enough financial runway to reach the point where its aircraft can become meaningful businesses.

Promotion

High conviction ACHR bulls now have this Tradr ETF

Joby generated $38.6 million in revenue in Q2, compared with just $5 million for Archer. Neither figure comes close to covering the companies’ expenses. Joby spent $28.3 million on the costs associated with generating that revenue, while selling, general and administrative (SG&A) expenses reached $76.5 million. R&D was the real heavyweight, at almost $195 million, leaving Joby with an operating loss of roughly $260 million.

Archer was in an even tougher position. Its $5 million of revenue came with $4.3 million in associated costs, while SG&A expenses approached $94 million and R&D spending reached $186 million. The result was an operating loss of around $279 million.

That level of spending is hardly shocking for companies attempting to establish an entirely new aviation category. The more important question is how long their balance sheets can support it. At the end of the quarter, Joby had approximately $2.2 billion in cash and investments, while Archer had around $1.5 billion.

On those figures alone, the investor sees Joby with a financial advantage. Maintaining its quarterly loss at roughly $260 million would give it around two years of runway, whereas Archer’s cash pile could cover only a little more than a year at its current burn rate.

However, the investor does not expect the situation to remain static. Joby has demonstrated autonomous flight technology in a cross-country test, while Archer has conducted manned flights between California airports. Those developments suggest both companies are getting closer to commercial operations.

Their relationships with established aviation companies should also be noted. Archer has Boeing as a partner, while Joby is working with Virgin Atlantic and Delta. Those relationships provide credibility and could potentially make future fundraising easier.

For the investor, however, neither stock is remotely close to being a sure thing. “Archer Aviation and Joby Aviation are high-risk stocks that only the most aggressive of growth investors should consider,” the 5-star investor explained. “But they are both making material progress as businesses, even as they continue to burn through cash at a rapid clip. That’s pretty normal for a start-up.” (To watch Gregg Brewer’s track record, click here)

Gregg Brewer’s take is that cash burn needs to be watched closely, but the bigger warning sign would be either company failing to replenish its reserves when necessary. If that happens, the investment case could change very quickly.

The Street sees the investment case for these stocks as somewhat different, although, ultimately, both boast plenty of upside. Joby only claims a Hold consensus rating, but its $11.50 average price target suggests shares will gain 98% in the months ahead. Archer claims a Strong Buy consensus rating, while its $11.60 average target offers one-year upside of 148%. (See JOBY stock forecast or ACHR stock forecast)

data.title: ‘SpaceX Stock Is in the Danger Zone,’ Says Investor
data.description:
SpaceX (NASDAQ:SPCX) stock has been surging again. Shares jumped almost 8% on Monday and are up in Tuesday’s session, extending a sharp rally that has taken the stock well above its early-August lows. The latest move has been fuelled by bullish Wall Street commentary, renewed anticipation around the next Starship launch and growing enthusiasm over SpaceX’s ambitions in AI and computing.

The rally is also putting the company’s valuation back under the spotlight. At around $2.2 trillion, SpaceX is already being valued on the assumption that its various businesses can deliver extraordinary growth. Investor Alaric Pow is far less convinced that the current valuation leaves enough room for disappointment.

The investor acknowledges that SpaceX is no longer simply a rocket company. Starlink has become a sizeable communications business, while SpaceX is pouring enormous sums into AI infrastructure and Starship, its next-generation reusable rocket designed to carry people and cargo into orbit. Revenue is growing rapidly, but so are the company’s capital requirements, leaving investors with a much more complicated question than simply whether SpaceX can keep expanding. Essentially, Pow believes the market is already placing enormous expectations on SpaceX, making the investment case much harder to justify.

Promotion

Two ETFs for long or short leverage on SPCX

The investor argues that SpaceX’s three businesses, Connectivity, Space and AI, need to be considered together. Starlink provides the company’s most established source of profits, while AI represents the biggest potential growth area. Starship could also lower launch costs and support the deployment of satellites and computing infrastructure. But these opportunities require substantial investment before they can generate the returns investors are expecting.

At the moment, Starlink is the least speculative part of the story. Connectivity generated $4.29 billion in Q2 revenue and $1.66 billion in operating income, showing that the satellite network can produce significant profits. Enterprise and government demand is also expanding rapidly. However, the investor points to a less encouraging trend: average revenue per subscriber has fallen as SpaceX has expanded into new markets and introduced cheaper plans. Subscriber growth has so far offset that decline, but there is no guarantee it will continue to do so indefinitely.

AI is where the $2.2 trillion valuation becomes particularly difficult to justify. The division generated $2.56 billion of Q2 revenue and about $1.15 billion of adjusted EBITDA, while SpaceX has secured $14.1 billion in contracted cloud sales. Yet the company is spending extraordinary amounts to build this infrastructure. Capital expenditure reached roughly $28.5 billion in the first half of 2026, of which about $23.6 billion for AI, while operating cash flow was only around $3.5 billion.

That gap is central to Pow’s argument. SpaceX has enough cash to fund the expansion for now, but eventually those investments need to produce substantial free cash flow.

Meanwhile, Starship adds another layer of uncertainty. Its first orbital revenue-generating mission was an important step, but reliability and rapid reusability remain unproven. The economic benefits could be significant if the programme succeeds, but investors are paying today for outcomes that have yet to be fully demonstrated.

“My conclusion on the company stock is somewhat counterintuitive,” Pow summed up. “I am highly constructive on SpaceX as a business but am considerably less constructive on SpaceX at the current share price.”

Accordingly, Pow rates SPCX stock a Sell. (To watch Pow’s track record, click here)

The mission was not flawless, however. One Raptor engine on the Super Heavy booster shut down during ascent, while another engine on the upper stage also experienced an early shutdown. SpaceX consequently shortened the mission and brought the spacecraft down after roughly three hours rather than completing the planned flight. Neither stage was recovered. GI considers those problems manageable for a first orbital attempt, particularly because Starship still completed its most important task: getting a substantial payload into orbit.

The payload itself is what makes Flight 14 especially significant. Third-party estimates put the combined mass of the 26 Starlink V3 satellites at roughly 52 tons. That is more than the Space Shuttle’s rated low-Earth-orbit payload and only about half of what a reusable Starship V3 is designed to carry. The 5-star investor sees that capacity as evidence that Starship could fundamentally change the economics and scale of commercial space activity.

More importantly, the cargo was part of SpaceX’s existing revenue-generating business. Each V3 satellite is designed to provide roughly 1 terabit per second (Tbps) of downlink capacity, meaning this mission potentially added around 26 Tbps to Starlink. Future Starship flights could carry substantially more. With SpaceX’s connectivity business already generating billions in quarterly revenue, GI believes Starship can now feed additional capacity into the segment that helps finance the company’s broader ambitions.

The same infrastructure could eventually support orbital AI computing. SpaceX has said AI compute satellites are planned for next year, although GI does not expect meaningful revenue from orbital data centers until at least 2028. The latest flight nevertheless provides the first tangible evidence that the launch infrastructure required for that opportunity is becoming viable.

GI’s biggest concerns remain Starship’s ability to achieve reliable reusability, improve engine reliability, and maintain the AI spending cycle that supports future orbital computing. Insider share unlocks and high interest rates could also pressure the stock.

Still, GI believes investors should focus less on short-term valuation and more on whether Starship works commercially. In his view, Flight 14 represents the first real step toward opening markets in orbital computing, manufacturing, lunar missions and other areas that remain largely inaccessible without a dramatically more capable and economical launch system.

Or, as GI puts it, buy SPCX shares now, and in 10 years, your kids will thank you for it when they see what Starship has made possible. (To watch Geneva Investor’s track record, click here)

On the Street, 27 analysts are also SPCX bulls, while an additional 4 Holds and 2 Sells can’t detract from a Strong Buy consensus rating. Going by the $235.10 average price target, a year from now, investors will be pocketing returns of 40%.  (See SPCX stock forecast)

data.title: Western Digital vs. Sandisk: One AI Storage Stock Is Good, the Other Is Better, Says Top Investor
data.description:
If you’re seeking out some of the biggest beneficiaries of the AI infrastructure buildout, then you need not look much further than Western Digital (NASDAQ:WDC) and Sandisk (NASDAQ:SNDK).  

These stocks have delivered extraordinary returns over the past year. The former has gained 253%, while the latter has surged a remarkable 1,311%.

Both are similar in the fact that they deal in computer storage, although they are exposed to different parts of the storage market, giving investors two distinct ways to play the enormous amount of storage hardware required by AI data centers. Western Digital is primarily a hard-drive company, while Sandisk – which was actually spun off from Western Digital at the start of 2025 – is focused largely on NAND flash memory and data-center storage.

Promotion

WDCX: an alternative to margin or options on WDC

Top investor Chris Neiger, who contributes to The Motley Fool and ranks among the top 1% of investors on TipRanks, recently weighed the two companies and their prospects as AI spending continues to reshape the storage industry.

Western Digital offers the more straightforward hard-drive investment. The company and Seagate control an estimated 85% of the HDD market, giving Western Digital a powerful position as data-center operators continue adding storage capacity.

Its fiscal fourth quarter provided plenty of evidence that demand remains strong. Revenue climbed 44% to $3.8 billion, while adjusted EPS more than doubled to $3.56. Strong demand has also given the company greater pricing power. Gross margin reached more than 54%, up 13 percentage points from the same period a year earlier.

The company also expects the momentum to continue. Management forecast first-quarter adjusted gross margin of about 55.5%, revenue of approximately $4.1 billion and adjusted EPS of around $4.

For Neiger, one attraction of Western Digital is the relative stability of its business. Hard-drive pricing and margins can still fluctuate, but the market tends to be less cyclical than flash memory. Meanwhile, AI data centers are generating enormous quantities of information that need to be stored. Over the next three years, Western Digital expects the volume of enterprise data to expand by at least 25% annually.

Sandisk offers something of a different proposition. Its business is heavily exposed to NAND flash, a form of memory that has become ever more important to AI infrastructure. A supply shortage has helped push prices and margins sharply higher.

In fiscal Q4 2026, Sandisk’s gross margin approached 85%, compared with roughly 27% a year earlier. Adjusted EPS exploded to $39.25 from just $0.29, while revenue jumped 372% to $8.9 billion.

Management expects another strong quarter. First-quarter revenue is projected at roughly $10.5 billion, representing 453% growth, while adjusted EPS is expected to reach $45. Gross margin is forecast to remain between 83% and 85%.

Neiger points to the enormous potential size of the NAND market as another reason to pay attention. Sandisk’s CFO expects the market to exceed $300 billion this year and approach $500 billion in 2027.

The catch is that NAND is a more cyclical business. If AI-related demand weakens sharply or supply catches up with demand, Sandisk’s exceptionally high margins could fall quickly.

Still, Neiger believes the AI infrastructure buildout has several years left to run. Estimates suggest global AI data-center capital spending could eventually touch $7 trillion by 2030, creating huge demand for the physical hardware needed to support the technology.

That leaves Sandisk with the greater upside potential, in Neiger’s view, because its high-margin NAND business could benefit more dramatically if AI infrastructure spending remains strong.

“I think that gives Sandisk the edge over Western Digital right now,” the 5-star investor summed up. “But if you tend to be a little more conservative in your tech investments and are looking for a pure hard drive play, Western Digital is still a great stock to own, too.” (To watch Neiger’s track record, click here)

The Street likes both of these stocks too, with the pair rated Strong Buys. WDC’s average price target stands at $664.47, a figure pointing to 12-month returns of 50%. SNDK, meanwhile, is expected to gain 28%, given its average target clocks in at $2,195.29. (See WDC stock forecast or SNDK stock forecast)

data.title: ‘Resist Temptation,’ Says Investor About Oracle Stock
data.description:
Oracle (NYSE:ORCL) has become one of the more unusual stories in the AI infrastructure trade. While hyperscaler peers Microsoft, Amazon, Alphabet and Meta remain close to their share price highs despite committing enormous sums to data centers and computing capacity, Oracle has fallen sharply from its 2025 peak, with the stock sitting 56% below the all-time high reached last September. The obvious question is whether that decline has created an opportunity or reflects a genuine financial problem.

The answer, according to investor Johnny Rice, who contributes to The Motley Fool, comes down less to Oracle’s growth than to what it is costing the company to achieve it.

Oracle’s business has been expanding rapidly, with revenue rising from $42.4 billion in fiscal 2022 to $67.4 billion in fiscal 2026. Much of the momentum is coming from Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, which provides the data-center capacity and computing power behind the AI boom. OCI revenue surged 121% year over year to $7.4 billion in fiscal 2027’s first quarter, compared with less than $1 billion during the same period four years earlier.

Promotion

Explore ORCZ for 2X short leverage on ORCL

Demand also looks substantial. Oracle’s RPO (remaining performance obligations), representing contracted revenue that has yet to be recognized, reached $664 billion at the end of the latest quarter. On the surface, that suggests the company has plenty of business waiting in the pipeline.

Rice’s concern is what Oracle has to spend to capture that opportunity. The company expects to spend roughly $95 billion on capital expenditures this year as part of the massive AI infrastructure buildout. That is a staggering amount for a company generating far less revenue than the other major hyperscalers.

The spending is already putting pressure on Oracle’s cash generation. Free cash flow was negative $5.4 billion in the latest quarter, while the company is generating only about 60 cents of cash for every dollar committed to capital expenditures. Rice points out that this represents a significant deterioration from Oracle’s historical financial profile.

With internal cash generation falling short, Oracle has been leaning heavily on financing. The company had $125 billion of long-term debt at the end of August, while another $288 billion of data-center lease commitments sit off the balance sheet. Additional project financing adds another layer of leverage to the AI expansion.

A recent dispute surrounding Project Jupiter highlights the risk. Oracle has sought protection from lease payments if the huge data-center project is delayed beyond its planned March 2028 completion date. If the facility is late and Oracle still has to make payments before the associated revenue arrives, its cash flow could come under further strain.

Rice acknowledges that other tech giants face similar pressures, but argues Oracle has far less financial cushion. “Oracle’s financial picture is much more precarious than the other four hyperscalers, and if the AI boom slows down — or worse — the consequences it faces will be much more severe,” the investor summed up. “Now, if everything goes according to plan, that could mean there is more upside for Oracle stock. I still don’t think it’s worth the risk.” (To watch Rice’s track record, click here)

Most Street analysts do think the risks are worth taking. Based on a mix of 27 Buys, 4 Holds and 1 Sell, the stock receives a Strong Buy consensus rating. Going by the $245.75 average price target, shares will be changing hands for a 71% premium a year from now. (See ORCL stock forecast)
